strengths: The results are reasonably well written up.
Enough details on the proposed algorithm.
*Originality*: The problem formulation and subsequent elaborations and conclusions appear novel.
*Quality*: The proposed solution is carefully devised to admit closed-form updates. With this goal in mind, all heuristics and approximations seem justified and well motivated.
*Clarity*: The paper is well organized and the ideas the authors want to convey are clearly exposed.
*Significance*: This work may shed a light on the problem of learning linear dynamical systems with sparse system matrices. It can also open new research lines in this regard.
The proposed algorithm is more useful for exploring the interacting laws of the LDSs than the classical ones.
The idea of imposing sparsity promoting priors to preserve structure of the system matrices for linear dynamical systems is interesting and possibly impactful.
The paper is well-motivated, with a thorough analysis of related work that situates the proposed method within the context of recent advances in LDS learning.
The mathematical derivations are sound, providing a solid theoretical foundation for the proposed approach.
weaknesses: The authors obtain an EM heuristic for the problem, but do not prove whether the EM heuristic provides good solutions or not.

The authors test their approach on two instances from "Database for the Identification of Systems" (http://homes.esat.kuleuven.be/~smc/daisy/), a well-known collection of 20+ instances, without explaining why they choose the two instances in particular. This smacks of cherry-picking.
The comparison against PEM and n4sid, which date back to 1970s and 1994, respectively, also does not seem to capture the current state of the art fully.

The authors do not consider any of the recent literature on learning of linear dynamical systems with side-constraints as a non-convex optimization problem (e.g. https://proceedings.mlr.press/v120/ahmadi20a, https://doi.org/10.1109/TAC.2023.3313351, https://hal.science/hal-04394297/document).
Novelty is rather limited which questions the overall contribution of the manuscript.

The real data section can be improved by further discussions; so far, only improved prediction errors are reported.

Section 2 could benefit from a literature review on sparse promoting methods. For example, what is the state-of-the-art of Lasso-like estimators? or, how do they compare to sparse Bayesian learning in this context? Specifically, the paper should discuss the limitations of using \ell_1 regularization for inducing sparsity, such as the non-differentiability at zero and the need for careful hyperparameter tuning. A comparison to reweighted \ell_1 minimization methods and their effectiveness in enhancing sparsity would also be beneficial. Furthermore, the review should delve into the advantages of sparse Bayesian learning (SBL), such as its ability to automatically learn hyperparameters and its probabilistic framework, and how these compare to the more deterministic approaches of Lasso-like methods. The discussion should also include specific examples of where SBL has been successfully applied to similar problems, highlighting both its strengths and potential drawbacks.

The heuristic method introduced in Section 3.2 is block coordinate descent (alternating minimization) rather than block coordinate gradient descent (BCGD). The authors should clarify why they chose alternating minimization instead of a true gradient‑based approach, especially given the non‑convex objective and the different convergence properties.
The main text does not seem to refer to Figure 1 anywhere; the reader would appreciate guidance about which ideas or explanations Figure 1 is supporting or complementing.

The authors may consider changing the notation of the normal probability distribution in eq. (7) from | to ; to align with the standardized notation encouraged by ICLR, and rename the matrix \boldsymbol{P} introduced in eq. (35) to avoid overlap with matrices \boldsymbol{P}^k_t and \boldsymbol{P}^k_{t,t-1} introduced earlier.

An appendix should be added explaining the derivative rule of structured matrices and why derivatives of unstructured matrices cannot be used in general; this should include how symmetry constraints affect derivative calculation and an example showing how using the incorrect rule can lead to non‑symmetric updates.
Appendix C could benefit from explaining how the mean and covariance of the noise \bar{\epsilon}_t are obtained.
The proposed algorithm cannot determine the order n of the system from data directly and the similarity transformation may shrink many parameters to very small values, leading to numerical errors.
The methodology more or less mirrors the development in "Sparse Bayesian Learning and the Relevance Vector Machine" article by Tipping. The novelty seems incremental.

Another of the authors' articles "An Iterative Min‑Min Optimization Method for Sparse Bayesian Learning" is very related to the present article; given the earlier works, the contribution of the present article becomes more incremental.

The authors claim that the priors promote structure of the matrices, but the explanation is not entirely convincing. It is not clear how sparsity‑promoting priors preserve the topological structure beyond setting some entries to zero, and the argument about similarity transformation being restricted to a generalized permutation matrix is not rigorously justified.

The definition of matrix sparsity could be clarified. While the authors introduce a sparsity‑promoting prior, it would be beneficial to show examples of what matrices look like after imposing the Student’s t‑distribution to better illustrate its effect, and a visualization or detailed explanation of the resulting non‑zero pattern would be helpful.

The applicability of this method in higher‑dimensional cases is unclear; the current experiments do not explore computational complexity or performance with increasing dimensionality, making it hard to assess scalability.

The paper is mathematically dense, which could challenge readers unfamiliar with LDSs. An additional table summarizing the notations would enhance readability and aid understanding for a broader audience.
The synthetic experiment in Section 5.1 appears overly simplified; additional experiments with more complex or higher‑dimensional system matrices are needed to validate the method’s effectiveness.
For the real‑world dataset experiments, it would be valuable to include datasets where the true underlying system matrices are known to enable direct comparison and assessment of structural accuracy.
